“We have started working to arrest those involved in the incident,” he said.

item.title: PM: Govt to establish six dedicated 100-bed hospitals for workers
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday told parliament that the government would establish six dedicated 100-bed hospitals in major industrial areas to ensure proper healthcare services for workers.
“To ensure proper medical care for workers and the working class, the government has planned to construct six hospitals, each with a capacity of 100 beds,” he said, adding that the hospitals will initially be established in Dhaka’s Savar and Ashulia, Gazipur’s Tongi and Kaliakair, Narayanganj and Chittagong.
The hospitals would be dedicated exclusively to workers, the prime minister said while replying to a lawmaker's question in parliament. “The hospitals will be named and developed specifically as healthcare facilities for workers.”
Earlier, raising the issue on a point of order, BNP lawmaker Shamsur Rahman Simul Biswas urged the prime minister to inform the house whether the government had any specific plan to establish hospitals in labor-intensive areas to ensure healthcare services for workers and their families.
He said they had heard from the labor minister about the prime minister's interest in ensuring healthcare services for low-income productive citizens, particularly working people.
At this point, Deputy Speaker Barrister Barrister Kayser Kamal said the lawmaker had raised the question ahead of the prime minister's question-answer session scheduled for Wednesday, as Tarique would not be present in the House on that day.
Responding to the query, the prime minister said Bangladesh's energy sector had been made dependent on foreign sources during more than a decade of authoritarian rule, with the country becoming reliant on imports instead of utilizing its own mineral resources for the benefit of its people.
He said the country's industrial development had also been hampered by import-dependent policies that prevented domestic industries from growing naturally.
Tarique said the country's healthcare system had similarly been gradually weakened during the previous autocratic regime, particularly in rural areas, where healthcare facilities established under earlier democratic governments had also been destroyed.
He said the Leader of the Opposition had also expressed concern over the country's healthcare system during a recent parliament session.
The prime minister said it was evident that the healthcare system had been deliberately destroyed during the authoritarian regime, forcing people of Bangladesh to go to a particular foreign country to seek medical treatment.
He said the current government had been elected by the people's votes and was working for people from all classes and professions. “The government is also giving importance to healthcare services for workers,” he added.

item.title: November rain brings signs of winter to Dhaka
item.description:
Residents of Dhaka experienced rainfall after a prolonged dry spell as rain accompanied by lightning began in different parts of the capital around 7pm on Monday.
Rain was reported in several areas, including Panthapath, Farmgate, Green Road, Banglamotor, Kalabagan and Dhanmondi.
According to the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), rainfall is likely in different parts of the country over the next few days, potentially bringing a slight drop in both daytime and nighttime temperatures.
The fall in nighttime temperatures may intensify the feeling of winter, although winter conditions have so far been more noticeable in the northern region. The department said there is little possibility of winter having a significant impact on other parts of the country at this time.
In a forecast issued at 6pm on November 9 for the subsequent 12 hours, the BMD said a low-pressure area was persisting in its normal position over the southwest Bay of Bengal, with an extended portion reaching the northeast Bay of Bengal.
The forecast said rain or thundershowers may occur at some places in Barisal, Chittagong and Rangpur divisions, and at 1 or 2 places in Rajshahi, Dhaka, Mymensingh, Khulna and Sylhet divisions.
During this period, both daytime and nighttime temperatures across the country may fall slightly.
The lowest temperature recorded in the country on Monday was 15°C in Tetulia, while Dhaka recorded 25°C.

item.title: Home minister: Govt verifying reports of Hasina’s passport, NID applications
item.description:
The government is examining reports that former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport and a national identity card (NID) in New Delhi, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Monday.
“The authenticity of the reports has not yet been verified. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Law are looking into the matter,” he told reporters at the secretariat.
Asked about reports in international media that Hasina, a fugitive convicted of crimes, had applied for the documents, the minister said the two ministries were examining the matter.
He said the authorities would assess the legal basis of the applications, whether they had been submitted properly and whether Hasina was legally eligible to obtain the documents.
Relevant provisions of the Passport Act, the Citizenship Act and laws governing NIDs would also be reviewed before the government made any official statement, he added.
On efforts to bring Hasina back to Bangladesh, Salahuddin said the government had already approached the country where she is staying through diplomatic channels under the existing extradition treaty.
“We have sent a letter through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in accordance with the extradition treaty, requesting that the convicted fugitive be returned to Bangladesh in accordance with the law,” he said.
Asked about recent crude bomb explosions, attacks on establishments and bus arson in the capital, the minister alleged that ousted political forces were carrying out such attacks to create instability.
Police would take legal action against those involved and deal firmly with such activities, he added.

item.title: Dengue claims five more lives, 2,260 hospitalised
item.description:
Five people died of dengue and 2,260 others were hospitalised across the country in the 24 hours to 8am on Monday, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
With the latest fatalities, the country’s dengue death toll has risen to 466 this year.
Of the five deaths, three were reported in Dhaka, while Mymensingh and Barisal divisions recorded one each.
Since January 1, a total of 152,173 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals nationwide. Of them, 145,593 have recovered.
Currently, 6,114 patients are receiving treatment at hospitals across the country.

item.title: Five MPs named to preside over parliament
item.description:
Five lawmakers have been nominated to the panel of chairpersons to conduct the fourth session of the 13th parliament.
Speaker Major (retd) Hafiz Uddin Ahmed announced their names at the opening sitting of the session, which began at 3:30pm on Monday. The speaker chaired the sitting.
The nominated members are Md Shahjahan of Noakhali-4, Sarwar Jamal Nizam of Chittagong-12, Muhammad Naushad Zamir of Panchagarh-1, Shahjahan Chowdhury of Chittagong-15, and reserved-seat MP Rasheda Begum Hira.
Under the Rules of Procedure of Parliament, members of the panel of chairpersons will preside over sittings in the absence of the speaker and the deputy speaker.

item.title: Writ seeks ban on primary school admission tests
item.description:
A writ petition has been filed seeking a ban on all forms of admission tests for primary school classes from Grade 2 to Grade 5, as well as on supplementary commercial textbooks not approved by the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB).
Lawyer Md Mahmudul Hasan Mamun filed the petition on Monday.
The respondents include the Cabinet secretary, the secretaries of the Secondary and Higher Education Division and the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education, the director general of the Directorate of Primary Education and the chairman of the NCTB.
The petition states that under the Primary Education (Compulsory) Act, 1990, every child has the legal right to unhindered admission to primary education. However, the government’s admission policy for students in government secondary schools subjects young children to competitive admission tests, which the petitioner claims contradicts the law and exceeds the government's legal authority.
It further argues that such tests create fear and cause mental distress among children.
The petition also alleges that educational institutions, in collusion with commercial publishers, are burdening students with supplementary textbooks and guidebooks beyond those approved by the NCTB, in violation of the National Curriculum and Textbook Board Act, 2018.
According to the petition, the excessive academic burden and weight of these books can harm children's physical health, including potentially damaging their spines, while discouraging independent thinking during their formative years.
It also cites the National Education Policy, 2010, which provides for one year of government-approved pre-primary education. However, kindergartens and other educational institutions have introduced additional levels, including Play, Nursery, KG-1 and KG-2, without government approval, the petition says.
The petitioner argues that these practices violate government directives and turn early childhood education into a commercial enterprise.

item.title: German Business Council holds 3rd AGM
item.description:
The German Business Council Trust (GBC) convened its 3rd Annual General Meeting (AGM) and Members' Business Networking Dinner on Saturday, November 8, at the Gold Room of The Westin Dhaka.
The high-level corporate gathering brought together the founding trustees, and distinguished members of the German Bangladeshi commercial community to review organizational progress and foster strategic bilateral economic collaboration.
The proceedings commenced in the late afternoon with the formal 3rd AGM session.
During the meeting, the GBC chairman Md Zahidul Islam presented an overview of the council’s annual operational achievements, statutory compliance updates, and future initiatives aimed at strengthening trade ties between Germany and Bangladesh.
GBC members engaged in an open floor Q&A session to discuss key business strategies, trust frameworks, and upcoming industry partnerships.
Following the internal meeting, the GBC hosted an exclusive networking reception and networking dinner.
Dr Rüdiger Lotz, Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to Bangladesh, attended as guest of honor.
In his keynote address, Lotz emphasized the expanding commercial synergy between Germany and Bangladesh, highlighting mutual opportunities in sustainability, trade expansion, and private sector investment.
The GBC chairman welcomed the ambassador, the board of trustees, and executive guests, reiterating the council’s commitment to serving as a vital platform for German businesses and local corporate stakeholders.
The evening concluded with an official group photograph, interactive business networking among attendees, and a dinner served at the Gold Room, followed by formal vote-of-thanks closing remarks.

item.title: Syed Tanvir Husain joins Banglalink as chief people officer
item.description:
Banglalink has appointed Syed Tanvir Husain as its chief people officer (CPO), further strengthening its leadership team as the company accelerates its transformation into a future-ready digital services organization.
He assumed the role on November 1, 2026, bringing more than three decades of diverse corporate experience, including over two decades in executive leadership positions.
A seasoned business and human resources leader, Tanvir brings extensive expertise in organizational transformation, strategic people management, leadership development, business growth, and workforce productivity.
Throughout his career, he has played pivotal roles in shaping organizational capabilities, driving transformation, and building high-performance cultures across telecommunications, technology, financial services, manufacturing, and diversified industries.
Prior to joining Banglalink, Tanvir served as divisional HR head – steel and consumer goods at Abul Khair Group.
Previously, he held the position of senior adviser at ACI Limited and served as chief growth officer at SSL Wireless, where he gained valuable experience in business strategy, growth, and digital transformation.
A significant chapter of his career was with Grameenphone, where he served as chief human resources officer for more than five years, contributing to the company's people strategy, leadership capabilities, and organizational transformation.
Earlier, he held senior leadership positions at Airtel Bangladesh as chief human resources officer, Citibank NA, and British American Tobacco Bangladesh, where he led the manufacturing HR function.
In his new role, Tanvir will spearhead Banglalink's people and organizational strategy, with a focus on strengthening leadership capabilities, accelerating talent development, enhancing workforce productivity, and fostering a high-performance, AI-first culture.
His leadership will be instrumental in building an agile, future-ready organization capable of supporting Banglalink's evolving business ambitions and sustainable growth.
Commenting on his appointment, Syed Tanvir Husain, CPO of Banglalink, said: "I am delighted to join Banglalink at such a defining stage of its journey. I believe meaningful transformation begins with people. By empowering our talent, strengthening leadership, and embracing AI as an enabler of productivity and innovation, we can build an organization that is agile, ambitious, and ready for the future. I look forward to working with my colleagues to foster a culture where people are inspired to challenge conventions, embrace change, and deliver exceptional business outcomes."
Banglalink welcomes Tanvir as its first chief people officer, reflecting the company's continued commitment to placing people, leadership, and organizational capability at the heart of its transformation.
His extensive cross-industry experience and proven leadership will play an important role in advancing Banglalink's ambition to become a leading digital services company.

item.title: Shahjalal Islami Bank holds financial inclusion workshop in Chuadanga
item.description:
Shahjalal Islami Bank PLC Organized a Seminar and Workshop on Financial Inclusion in Chuadanga on Sunday, November 8, at the premises of the non-governmental development organization 'Atmobishwash' on College Road of Chuadanga.
The program was cashless transactions via 'Bangla QR,' methods for small-scale and aspiring female entrepreneurs to access bank financing, and financial literacy and agricultural financing for farmers.
Managing director of Shahjalal Islami Bank PLC Mosleh Uddin Ahmed presided over in the program, while director of the Bangladesh Bank Rajshahi Office Md Nazim Uddin was present as chief guest.
Additional director of the Bangladesh Bank Rajshahi Office AKM Amirul Islam delivered a presentation on Bangla QR.
At the end of the event, agricultural financing cheques were formally handed over to the farmers.
Among others, head of the agriculture investment and sustainable finance department at Shahjalal Islami Bank PLC Md Abdur Rahim along with other officials were present at the program.
The program was moderated by Md Manzur Rahman, AVP of the bank’s sustainable finance department.

item.title: Crude bomb explosions at multiple locations in Gopalganj
item.description:
A series of crude bomb explosions at several key locations in Gopalganj on Monday night triggered panic among residents amid a programme called by a banned organisation.
Police have stepped up security across the district to prevent further incidents and maintain law and order.
According to local sources, crude bombs were detonated near the main gate of Gopalganj District School, along the boundary walls of the Government Women's College and passport office, and in front of the Government Technical School and College.
The blasts caused panic among residents in the surrounding areas.
In a separate incident, a crude bomb exploded beside the Upazila Muktijoddha Complex in Kotalipara at around 9:15pm. A group of miscreants arrived on motorcycles, detonated the bomb and fled the scene.
No casualties or damage were reported.
Kotalipara Fire Service Station Master Sirajul Islam confirmed the explosion, saying the bomb went off in an open space in front of the complex.
He said a generator at Café Ekattor, located behind the complex, caught fire shortly afterwards due to overheating. Fire service personnel rushed to the spot and brought the blaze under control. However, he clarified that there was no connection between the bomb explosion and the generator fire.
Law enforcement personnel rushed to the locations following the incidents. Police have increased patrols and tightened security across the district to prevent further disturbances.
No casualties have been reported in any of the incidents so far.

item.title: Crude bomb explodes at JnU, one suspect detained
item.description:
A crude bomb exploded in the parking area near the second gate of Jagannath University (JnU) on Monday evening, prompting the university's Chhatra Dal unit to detain a suspected individual.
The explosion occurred at around 7:30pm between two buses parked near the gate. The detainee was identified as Rezwan Ahmed, a student of the Department of Psychology from the 2021-22 academic session. Preliminary information suggests that he is an activist of the university's Chhatra League.
Eyewitnesses said they heard a loud bang at around 7:30pm, followed by smoke rising from the area. The blast occurred between two parked buses near the university's second gate.
However, no one was seen at the scene immediately after the explosion, they added.
University Proctor Professor Nasir Ahmad said they had heard about the explosion near the second gate while it was raining in the evening.
"We were not on campus at the time. We will review the CCTV footage to identify those involved," he said.
Regarding the detention, the proctor said the university's Chhatra Dal unit had detained a suspect and that they had contacted the police.

item.title: Six AL activists arrested while hurling crude bombs in Dhaka
item.description:
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) have arrested six activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations while they were allegedly hurling crude bombs in different parts of the capital. Three crude bombs and a motorcycle were recovered from their possession.
The DMP media division disclosed the information on Monday night.
A series of crude bombs explosions have rocked different parts of the capital over the past few days. Several explosions and incidents of bus arson were also reported at different locations on Monday.
Amid the spate of incidents, law enforcement agencies have tightened security across the capital.

item.title: Ahsan's 152, Tafiul’s 7-for steer Bangladesh U19s into Asia Cup semis
item.description:
Bangladesh Under-19 team stormed into the semifinals of the Under-19 Asia Cup with a crushing 205-run victory over Malaysia on Monday after Ahsan Al Mumin's unbeaten 152 and Tafiul Alam Tamim's seven-wicket haul today at Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Oman.
Bangladesh posted 303-8 in 50 overs after winning the toss and electing to bat, before bowling out Malaysia for just 98 in 30.5 overs.
Ahsan was the standout performer with the bat, smashing an unbeaten 152 off 133 balls, including 10 fours and six sixes.
Robiul Hasan Anik provided valuable support with 45 off 48 balls as Bangladesh recovered from an early setback to post a formidable total.
Malaysia's Nagineswaran Sathnakumaran, Syahir Asyraf and Aulga Gunawan claimed two wickets apiece.
In reply, Malaysia's batting line-up had no answer to Tafiul's devastating spell. The right-arm bowler claimed seven wickets for just 18 runs in 7.5 overs, including two maiden overs, to dismantle the opposition.
Nagineswaran offered some resistance with 50 off 81 balls but received little support from his teammates.
Rubay Islam Rizon complemented Tamim's effort with two wickets as Bangladesh completed a comprehensive victory to secure their semifinal berth. Their semifinal opponents are yet to be confirmed.

item.title: Bad light forces draw in Sylhet as West Indies take series
item.description:
Bad light ended the second Test between Bangladesh and West Indies in a draw in Sylhet on Monday, handing the visitors a 1-0 series win.
Bangladesh were 184 for four in their chase of 369 when bad light stopped play before 2:45pm on the final day. They still needed 185 runs, while West Indies needed six wickets.
The umpires were due to inspect the light at 4pm, but the two captains agreed to a draw before that. West Indies had won the first Test in Mirpur by eight wickets.
Towhid Hridoy, who scored an unbeaten 242 in the first innings, followed it with 82 and was named player of the match. He became the first Bangladesh batter to score a double century and a fifty in the same Test.
West Indies left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican was named player of the series for his 16 wickets, nine in the first Test and seven in the second.
West Indies resumed on 345 for three, added 53 runs in 10 overs and declared on 398 for six. Kavem Hodge made 142, his third Test century, while Kevin Wickham scored 78 and Brendon King 61.
Nayeem Hasan took two for 72, Mehidy Hasan Miraz two for 85 and Taijul Islam two for 118.
Bangladesh lost both openers before lunch. Tanzid Hasan was caught at the midwicket boundary for 21 trying to hit Warrican for six. Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto was given lbw for 14 off Warrican after a West Indies review, leaving Bangladesh on 40 for two.
Hridoy and Mushfiqur Rahim then batted through the entire second session without losing a wicket, adding 113 runs in 34 overs. Their third-wicket stand was worth 135 runs.
During the innings, Mushfiqur became the first Bangladesh batter to score 7,000 Test runs. He reached the mark with a single off Warrican in the 20th over. Mominul Haque is second on the list with 5,293 runs.
Bangladesh lost both set batters within the first nine overs after tea. Hridoy was bowled for 82 trying to sweep Warrican, missing a full delivery from over the wicket that pitched well outside leg stump. It was Warrican's 100th Test wicket.
Mushfiqur fell one short of his fifty when Shamar Joseph bowled him for 49 off 123 balls. Litton Das and Miraz were at the crease when the light faded.
"Apart from Hridoy, nobody batted well in the first innings, and we paid the price for that," Shanto said after the match.
Hridoy spoke about batting with Mushfiqur. "I've followed Mushi bhai since childhood. He is my idol, and I always try to learn from him," he said.
Bangladesh made 386 in their first innings in reply to West Indies' 356, with pacer Hasan Mahmud taking six for 90.
Bangladesh fly to South Africa on Tuesday for a two-Test series. The first Test begins in Johannesburg on November 15.

item.title: Hamza joins Bangladesh team for remaining SAFF fixtures
item.description:
Hamza Choudhury has arrived in Bangladesh on Monday to join the national team ahead of their remaining fixtures in the TECNO SAFF Championship 2026.
The Leicester City midfielder, currently on loan at English Championship side Sheffield United, was received by Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) Executive Committee Member and Team Manager Amirul Islam Babu, along with BFF Executive Committee Member and National Teams Committee Member Imteaz Hamid Shobuj.
Hamza missed Bangladesh's opening Group A fixture against Bhutan as he was unable to join the squad earlier due to his club commitments in England, with the FIFA international window not yet open.
The midfielder's arrival is expected to provide a major boost to the Bangladesh side ahead of their second and final group match against Sri Lanka on Wednesday.
Bangladesh began their campaign with a 1-0 victory over Bhutan at the National Stadium in Dhaka on Thursday, with substitute Mohammad Ibrahim scoring the decisive goal in the 69th minute.
The men in red and green have already secured their place in the semi-finals after Bhutan and Sri Lanka played out a 2-2 draw in their Group A encounter on Sunday.
Bangladesh will now look to finish the group stage on a high, with a victory over Sri Lanka ensuring they advance to the knockouts as group winners.

item.title: Eric Mare named interim Bangladesh women’s team coach
item.description:
The Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) on Monday appointed Eric Mare as interim head coach of the national women’s football team for a one-month assignment, with regular coach Peter Butler undergoing cancer treatment in England.
Mare will take charge of the team as the reigning SAFF champions prepare for their upcoming international commitments against Singapore, the BFF announced in a statement.
“The Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) is pleased to announce the appointment of Mr. Eric Mare as the Interim Head Coach of the Bangladesh Women’s National Football Team for a one-month assignment,” the statement read.
The women’s team is currently training in a camp ahead of two friendly matches against Singapore on December 1 and 5.
Earlier on Sunday, Butler informed the media that he had been diagnosed with cancer. The English coach also revealed that the BFF had sought his permission to appoint an interim coach during his absence, which he granted.
Butler, however, expressed his determination to fight the disease and return to Bangladesh to resume his coaching duties.
Meanwhile, the BFF extended its best wishes to Butler for a speedy recovery.
“The BFF extends its heartfelt best wishes to Mr. Peter Butler, Head Coach of the Bangladesh Women’s National Team, for a speedy and full recovery. We sincerely hope he regains his health soon and rejoins the team,” the statement added.

item.title: Mushfiqur becomes first Bangladesh batter to score 7,000 Test runs
item.description:
Mushfiqur Rahim became the first Bangladeshi cricketer to reach 7,000 runs in Test cricket, achieving the milestone with a single off Roston Chase in the 20th over of Bangladesh’s second innings on the fifth day of their Test against the West Indies at Sylhet International Cricket Stadium on Monday.
Bangladesh were chasing 369 for victory, with Mushfiqur and Towhid Hridoy anchoring the innings in a third-wicket partnership.
Mushfiqur brought up the landmark with a single to mid-on off an angling length delivery from Chase, etching his name into the record books.
Bangladesh’s most-capped Test cricketer also holds the national record for the most Test centuries.
Mushfiqur, who missed the first Test of the series after sustaining a finger injury, was also the first Bangladesh batter to reach 5,000 and 6,000 runs in the longest format.
Mominul Haque and the now-retired Tamim Iqbal occupy the second and third positions behind Mushfiqur on Bangladesh’s all-time Test run-scoring list.
The two are also behind Mushfiqur among Bangladesh’s highest century-makers in Tests. Mushfiqur has 14 centuries, including a career-best 219 not out, which was the country’s highest individual Test score before Hridoy surpassed it with an unbeaten 242 earlier in the Sylhet Test.
Mominul and Tamim have 13 and 10 Test centuries respectively.
Having made his international debut in 2005, Mushfiqur is Bangladesh’s most experienced Test cricketer. He was playing his 107th Test, having become the first Bangladeshi to feature in 100 Tests in November 2025.
Mushfiqur was eventually bowled by Shamar Joseph for 49, narrowly missing out on his 31st Test half-century, as Bangladesh reached 183 for four in the 57th over.

item.title: Trump says deportation policy was ‘too tough’ for voters
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Sunday said that his deportation policy for undocumented immigrants was “too tough” for voters and he can work with the Democrats in the new Congress to craft an immigration deal.
Speaking during his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm election, Trump said his deportation policy may have been part of the reason Republicans lost.
“I think it was too tough,” Trump said. “I think it might be too tough, yeah. And a lot of people would say that it’s great. But a lot of people think it’s too tough.”
In his interview to CBS that aired on Sunday, Trump said that he can find a way to work with the Democrats.
“The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it’s something — I think that’s something that’s actually doable,” he said in the interview.
Trump did not share the details of what the immigration deal would look like but shortly after the interview he appointed Stephen Miller, who designed the Trump administration’s hardline deportation policy, as his chief of staff.
In his tenure, Trump’s administration has aggressively pushed to deport millions of undocumented migrants which drew widespread criticism.
Trump said he was just joking about making Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) boss Dana White his next White House press secretary.
“I was only kidding, but Dana loves the idea,” Trump told reporters.
In a social media post Saturday, Trump implored White to accept his offer, writing, “Dana, please take the job!” and calling him a “violent fighter and warrior.”
White is a long-time friend of Trump. He has maintained silence on Trump’s remarks, saying that he would “have more to talk about” after meeting with Trump on Monday.
The position of the press secretary has been vacant since Katie Zacharia left on October 16 after less than a week on the job.
Trump on Sunday said that he will be meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin ‌at an ⁠APEC ⁠leaders’ summit in China next week to discuss ending the Iran war.
Before flying back to Washington from Florida, Trump while speaking to the media said: “One of the meetings, I think, will be with ‌President Putin and President Xi, and that’ll be ‌interesting. ​We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we’ll be talking a lot of things. We’re trying to end the ​war in Iran.”
Russia in October has said that this first of its kind trilateral meeting is “being prepared.”
While Trump has mentioned denuclearization as the focus of the meeting, a Wall Street Journal report said that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
In his interview with CBS Trump said that “I believe we’re very close to ⁠making a ​deal” to end the Russia-Ukraine war that would result in a “little bit different shape Ukraine,” without sharing any further details.

item.title: Twenty migrants die trying to reach Greece’s Crete
item.description:
Twenty people have died over the weekend trying to reach Greece’s island of Crete, which has become a main destination for migrants headed for the European Union, authorities said on Monday.
Eight bodies were found on one boat and 12 on another, while some 40 people were rescued off both, the Greek coast guard said on Monday.
Maritime police launched an emergency rescue late Saturday after a boat issued an alarm signal, with strong winds making sea conditions difficult, the coast guard said.
Around 28 survivors and one body, all Sudanese nationals, were picked up by another boat sailing nearby, then transferred to a police vessel and taken to Crete, authorities had said on Sunday.
Two Sudanese citizens, one of them 16, were arrested after being identified by the survivors as suspected people-smugglers, the authorities said.
During the night from Sunday to Monday, the coast guard found their boat, with seven additional bodies on board, it said.
In a separate incident, 12 bodies were found on a boat south of the island on Monday, while 18 people were rescued, the coast guard said.
In all, the Greek coast guard and the EU’s Frontex border agency rescued a total of 105 on Monday, according to the port authorities.
Crete has become one of the main entry points into the European Union for migrants departing from Libya and attempting the dangerous crossing to Greece.
Many of the attempted crossings turn deadly when the vessels sink or run into trouble.
According to the United Nations refugee agency, more than 37,000 migrants have arrived in Greece in 2026 so far.
Over 22,000 of those people landed on Crete, the country’s largest island.
In response to that influx, the government has announced plans to open a temporary housing complex near Heraklion, the island’s largest city.

item.title: Indian capital chokes with pollution after Diwali fireworks
item.description:
Toxic air in parts of India’s capital New Delhi soared to more than 58 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily limit Monday, after fireworks for the Hindu festival of Diwali, air monitor data showed.
Millions celebrate the annual festival of lights with fireworks in one of the world’s most polluted capitals, worsening winter smog fueled by vehicle emissions, farm fires and industry.
The Supreme Court this month allowed the limited use of so-called “green” firecrackers, designed to produce fewer emissions, during Diwali.
But restrictions are routinely flouted, with the city reverberating with explosions.
On early Monday morning, around eight hours after the peak of the bursting fireworks, levels of cancer-causing PM 2.5 microparticles hit 879 micrograms per cubic meter in the Mandir Marg locality, according to monitoring organization IQAir, which cited data from a city government station.
That is nearly 59 times the WHO’s recommended daily maximum.
Authorities have in recent weeks implemented restrictions on traffic and construction as they seek to curb smog in New Delhi, home to more than 30 million people.
Vehicles account for 23% of Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20%, according to India’s environment ministry.
Industry, including coal-fired power plants, contributes about nine percent.
The largest share, 27%, comes from secondary particles, formed when gases released by vehicles, industry, power plants and biomass burning react in the atmosphere.
A 2024 study published in The Lancet Planetary Health, a peer-reviewed research journal, estimated that 3.8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution.

item.title: Saudi authorities briefly warn of ‘aerial threat’ in Riyadh
item.description:
Saudi authorities briefly warned residents of the capital Riyadh of an aerial threat on Monday, a day after an attack on its business district.
“Warning. The area is under a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors, and follow the instructions of Civil Defense,” the message said, before lifting the warning minutes later.
Saudi Arabia has faced near-daily strikes since October, when the Houthis intensified their campaign against the kingdom after ousting Riyadh-backed government forces from their positions on the Red Sea coast.
On Sunday, the Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh’s business district, where witnesses said a skyscraper belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco was damaged.
Saudi authorities said the building had been “subjected to an attempted attack.”
Aramco facilities have been repeatedly struck by the Houthis in recent months, with tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company headquarters all targeted by the group.
A 2022 truce that had paused fighting in Yemen’s long-running conflict fell apart in July, and Saudi Arabia has since traded blows with the Houthis, who have struck Saudi airports and military sites as well as energy infrastructure.

item.title: Trump says Iran war ‘highly unlikely’ to resume
item.description:
US President Donald Trump cast doubt on renewed fighting with Iran, telling CNN it was “highly unlikely,” ahead of a meeting with mediator Qatar’s prime minister on Monday.
Trump has threatened to resume strikes in recent weeks, with US media reports suggesting that hostilities could restart after last Tuesday’s midterm elections.
The president told CNN in an interview on Sunday that renewed fighting was “highly unlikely,” but warned that his decision “depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement.”
“I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them,” he said.
Trump is scheduled to meet Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who is also the country’s foreign minister, at the White House on Monday.
The meeting will be Trump’s first with a foreign leader since a massive midterm loss that saw his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi suggested on Sunday that peace talks had been paused while the political fallout of the vote was being assessed.
“For the past few days, there has been no more travel (by mediators), and the reason for this is the shock that the election results in the United States have caused to everyone,” Araghchi told state television.
“We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward,” he added.
Trump has acknowledged that the highly unpopular war with Iran -- which began with US-Israeli strikes in late February -- was at least partially responsible for the Republicans’ defeat.
Araghchi said Monday that the US president “clearly recognizes that the vast majority of Americans are disgusted with Israel.”
“Americans are evidently sick and tired of Israel bamboozling US administrations into Forever Wars,” Araghchi said on X. “They had enough. So has our region.”
In Sunday’s CNN interview, Trump once again suggested that the economic pressure Iran is under will force its leaders into accepting the United States’ terms.
“They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation,” Trump claimed. “They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off.”
Iran’s official figures put inflation at nearly 90% year-on-year in September.
Iranian state television said the island of Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz was attacked overnight Sunday, hours after the official IRNA news agency reported two explosions there.
Various regional powers, including Qatar and Pakistan, have been trying for months without success to bring a definitive halt to the war.
Outright fighting has largely subsided, but Iran continues in its efforts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, vital to global energy supplies, while the US Navy maintains its own counterblockade of Iranian ports.

item.title: G7 ministers to press Rubio on Iran, Ukraine at Paris talks
item.description:
European top diplomats were on Monday set to press US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to ensure any settlement in the war with Russia is fair to Ukraine and steer clear of any new escalation with Iran, at talks of the G7 group in Paris.
The meeting of ministers from the leading industrialized nations of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States will provide Europe and its allies with a chance to air preoccupations with their US counterpart.
Russia’s war against Ukraine following the February 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbor is grinding towards its fifth anniversary. And Washington is still not ruling out new attacks against Iran even after the defeat of President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the midterms.
The meeting coincides with US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday on ending the Ukraine war, with Europe concerned Kyiv must not be forced to accept disadvantageous conditions and that the US could offer Russia new security guarantees over the heads of the Europeans.
“For Europe, it is clear: we do not need to establish a new security architecture for Europe,” said German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul as he headed to the talks, adding Europe “must have a place at the table.”
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Sunday that Europeans will be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks, with France also participating.
Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a “very big” deal with Russia involving not only Ukraine but “all of Europe.”
But before leaving for Paris, Rubio said the post-war security infrastructure of Europe is “one of the key topics that’s been raised repeatedly in every conversation any time negotiations have been discussed.”
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he noted.
On Iran, Trump has not ruled out new strikes, including at so-called Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
Europeans, however, are eager to see a resolution and shipping traffic return to normal in the Strait of Hormuz energy transit hub.
Trump allayed some fears by telling CNN it was “highly unlikely” that fighting would resume.
“We certainly cannot afford any military escalation at this point,” said Wadephul, adding the G7 talks would “focus on identifying ways to ensure it is indeed avoided.”
Rubio warned however there had been “no progress” in talks with Iran whose demands he said were “simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”
The G7 ministerial meeting, one of the final acts of the French G7 presidency that saw President Emmanuel Macron host Trump for the leaders’ summit this summer in the lakeside resort of Evian, had long been scheduled to be held in the southern port city of Marseille.
But at the last minute the event was moved to Paris, with only scheduling reasons given for the change.
The visit by Rubio -- seen by US media as a potential candidate to succeed Trump -- is his first abroad since the midterms. Washington will in 2027 take over the G7 presidency from France.
“It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country,” Rubio said, alluding to the fact that Trump will now see both houses of Congress controlled by the Democrats.
The sidelines of the meeting will also see the French finance ministry hosting on Monday a donor conference to raise funds to repair the dome protecting the nuclear reactor that exploded in Ukraine’s Chernobyl in 1986 after it was damaged in a Russian strike last year.
Around 500 million euros is required but only just over half has been raised so far, with a target date of spring 2027 to muster the rest of the funds, the French finance ministry told AFP.
Even though the meeting was moved to Paris, Marseille will still host the launch of a network of 14 global ports uniting to combat drug trafficking, which has become a major scourge in the southern city, Barrot said.

item.title: Universities brace for enrolment slump
item.description:
The country's higher education institutions may soon face a growing student shortage, particularly among private universities, as the number of seats available is more than double the number of students who passed this year's Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) and equivalent examinations.
Although there is no overall shortage of seats in higher education, smaller, mid-tier and less-established private universities, especially those outside Dhaka, may face mounting difficulties in attracting students. Some public universities could also struggle to fill their seats, educationists and sector insiders believe.
According to the University Grants Commission (UGC), the country has 61 public universities and affiliated institutions offering a combined 1,082,288 undergraduate seats. Of these, public universities account for 101,862 seats, while 107 private universities have a capacity of around 410,000 students.
This brings the total number of seats in higher education institutions to 1,492,288.
In comparison, only 646,685 students passed this year's HSC and equivalent examinations, leaving 845,603 more seats than successful candidates. The available seats are therefore more than twice the number of students who qualified for higher education.
The figures may change slightly after the results of applications for re-evaluation of examination scripts are published.
However, not all successful candidates will pursue higher education. Once admissions to public universities, National University-affiliated colleges, medical and dental colleges, and engineering institutions are completed, the pool of prospective students for private universities will shrink further, intensifying competition among them.
Private university representatives say established institutions are unlikely to face major difficulties, but newer, mid-tier and less-known universities may come under considerable pressure. Institutions outside Dhaka could find it particularly difficult to attract students.
A decline in enrolment could affect their revenue, payment of teachers and staff salaries, and the continuation of academic activities.
A UGC report published in 2024, based on 2022 data, found that 38.2% of seats in private universities remained vacant. Between 2018 and 2021, an average of 60.8% of their seats went unfilled. The problem was more pronounced among universities outside Dhaka, raising concerns that the lower number of HSC graduates this year could worsen the situation.
Educationists say students' preferences depend not only on seat availability but also on institutional reputation, academic standards, subject choices, tuition fees and location. As a result, some universities may fill their seats while many others continue to have significant vacancies.
Educationist Rasheda K Chowdhury said vacant seats in universities were not a new phenomenon but a longstanding trend that had become more visible following this year's HSC results.
She said approvals had been granted for numerous public and private universities without adequately assessing student demand.
"Only around 10 private universities in the country can be considered reasonably good in terms of quality. Many of the others have turned into certificate-selling factories," she said, warning that the situation would worsen unless these institutions were brought under proper control.
She also pointed out that access to technical universities and polytechnics remained limited despite their importance, calling for a policy framework to restore discipline and improve the quality of existing institutions rather than establish more universities.
Poet, essayist, researcher and academic Dr Shoaib Zibran said higher education should expand in the shape of a pyramid, with more students at primary and secondary levels and progressively fewer at higher levels.
"Bangladesh has followed the opposite path. The number of higher education institutions and seats has expanded far beyond actual demand," he said.
He attributed the trend to historical and political factors, including an excessive emphasis on degrees and the use of university establishments by local politicians as a means of gaining prestige and influence without assessing actual needs.
Dr Zibran also expressed concern over the weak academic foundations of many HSC graduates, citing disruptions caused by the Covid-19 pandemic, automatic promotions, the July uprising and repeated changes to the curriculum introduced in 2021.
He warned that admitting students to higher education without addressing these learning gaps could deepen the problem.
Universities might also lower admission standards to fill vacant seats, allowing students with weak academic foundations to enter institutions with poor educational standards. This could eventually produce a less-skilled generation entering the job market, he added.
He called for a more balanced education system, with greater emphasis on technical and vocational education rather than pushing everyone towards university degrees.
"Not everyone needs higher education. It should be available to those pursuing research, policymaking, critical thinking and knowledge creation. The economy also needs skilled workers, so students should be guided towards technical and vocational education based on their abilities and interests," he said.
UGC member Professor Dr Abdullah Al Mamun said the current situation was the consequence of a longstanding culture of prioritising certificates and pass rates over educational standards.
He said political appeasement and the tendency to satisfy all stakeholders had damaged the education system.
The situation should serve as a warning to both public and private universities, he said, urging all institutions to prioritise academic quality.
"Although the country has more than 100 private universities, only a handful are considered good. Those institutions will not face a shortage of students. We hope others will focus on improving educational standards," he said.
He added that the government's goal was to ensure skills-based and knowledge-based education so that graduates could find employment.
Regarding university approvals, Abdullah Al Mamun said many institutions had been established in the past without properly assessing their necessity, demand or capacity.
He said the government was now working to restore discipline in the education sector and had no plans to approve new universities unless there was a specific need for specialised institutions.
Alongside improving public universities, the UGC is also working to enhance academic standards at private universities and strengthen legal oversight, he added.

item.title: ULAB observes National Revolution and Solidarity Day with a discussion program
item.description:
The University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB) observed National Revolution and Solidarity Day on 9 November, 2026 through a discussion program highlighting the historical significance and national impact of the Sepoy-People's Uprising of 7 November 1975.
The program began with the national anthem and patriotic songs performed by members of the ULAB Cultural Forum Prof Dr Milan Kumar Bhattacharjee, acting vice-chancellor of ULAB, delivered the welcome address, highlighting the day's historical significance and its relevance to Bangladesh's national history.
A documentary on the historical background and sequence of events surrounding National Revolution and Solidarity Day was also screened.
The main segment featured a panel discussion exploring the historical context, significance, and different dimensions of the day. The session was moderated by Abantee Harun, assistant professor of the Department of General Education and director of the Centre for South Asian Studies at ULAB.
The program concluded with closing remarks by Prof Dr Muhammad Golam Kibria, Dean of the School of Science and Engineering at ULAB. Sirajum Munira Joti, a lecturer at the Centre for Language Studies, hosted the event.
Faculty members, university officials, students, and distinguished guests attended the program. The event concluded with a vote of thanks emphasizing the importance of understanding historical events and drawing lessons from the past.

item.title: A flower garden beyond the river
item.description:
I heard them before I saw them.
Counting together. One, two, three, four. It rose out of the hills so clearly that I stopped walking to listen.
I had been walking for a long time by then. My legs were tired, and my shoes were soaked, but the counting pulled me forward like a hand.
You leave the road and go on foot, about four kilometers, into the hills of Lama, in Bandarban. You wade a river. You cross spring after spring, some at your knees, some deeper. Where someone could, they laid a bamboo bridge. Where they couldn’t, there is only a tree trunk, cut down and left across the water. You step onto it and try not to look down.
And then, at the end, there is a bamboo school. Open windows. Children in uniforms upstairs counting.
I had come to see what a school looks like when everything about it is so hard to reach, even the money to keep it open. What I found was a room full of students with eyes full of hope.
In the Mro language, Pawmum Tharkla means "flower garden."
In 2016, it was one small room on a hilltop, surrounded by four villages. Two men, Shahriar Parvez and Man Rong Mro, had come to Lama for a different project. They found villages full of children and no school at all. The Karbari, the local headman, gave the land and chose the name. And the school, Pawmum Tharkla, was born.
The founder, Shahriar Parvez, remembers those first days clearly: “The children had no formal way of getting an education. They played, and the days slipped by with nothing in them. No books, no classroom.”
“Nothing to do” was not a phase for them. It was their childhood.
He was still a student when he began. At first, he says, he simply thought it would be good for the community. He had no grand plan, only a feeling that he could not walk away from what he had seen.
Then something shifted. The idea became a responsibility, and the responsibility became a part of his life. The better he got to know the people, the more it pulled at him.
Today, he says, they are his family.
You can hear it in the way he talks about them. He does not speak of a project. He speaks of people he loves and cares for.
So they built a school from what the hills already gave.
No brick. No concrete.
Bamboo, wood, teak, and thatch; about 1,000 pieces of baijya and 15,000 of paya, and nearly half of it donated by the villagers themselves. Families who had almost nothing gave what they had, because this was their children’s school, their future.
The main building rises 25 feet under a thatched roof 52 feet long. Beside it is an open amphitheater, built for the whole community to gather. There is room for about 100 children. For now, there are 76. And it is the only school that four small paras have.
The children learn in Krama, the Mro script, and Bangla, alongside English, math, and science. They learn handicrafts, sustainable farming, and self-defense. They learn to be Mro and Bangladeshi at the same time.
Children in class at Pawmum Tharkla School. Photo: Shuchi Binte Shahjalal
Three teachers hold all of it up. Man Kong Mro teaches English. Puk Duk teaches the mother tongue. Reng Wai teaches math, and when the day is done, he goes on to care for the hostel.
Almost every one of them earns less than Tk10,000 a month. But still they stay. They are dedicated, and each does whatever they can from their side.
Some kinds of love do not come with a salary.
Grade one has 23 children. Grade two has 24. Then it begins to thin. Where did the others go?
Maybe the school was small when its oldest classes began. It is only nine years old. But money is part of the answer.
Education here costs nothing. The hostel, which opened two years ago, does. A boarding child is spared the long walk home, which turns cruel in the rains, but the fee climbs gradually with each class: less in grades one and two and up to Tk 12,000 a year by grade five. For most families here, even that is more than they can pay.
Behind every empty chair, I think, is a family doing arithmetic no parent should have to do.
Out here, you understand how far this place is from everything.
If someone falls sick, there is no road. They are carried the whole four kilometers on foot. In the rainy season, the paths turn to slick mud, and the bamboo bridges sometimes collapse. I kept imagining a sick person, carried across the water, one slow step at a time.
For the families here, that is not imagination. It is a fear they carry every monsoon.
In front of the school stands one tubewell. It works, and it never rests, because there is no other clean water. The only other source is a spring, shared by the whole community. The children bathe and wash in it.
We were told the spring water carries disease. A doctor on our team provided free care and found scurvy and skin diseases among the children. Scurvy comes from too little vitamin C in the diet. The skin diseases were linked to the shared water.
The school runs on crowdfunding. The founders were told a school not registered in a government name would never get a state grant.
To register it or move the land into a government name would cost money they do not have. So it stands because people keep choosing, again and again, to keep it standing. Strangers, supporters, villagers, teachers.
Each one a small yes.
Before I left, I spoke with a boy of about eleven or twelve, Kain Pong Morung.
Kain Pong Morung, a student of Pawmum Tharkla School in Lama, Bandarban. Photo: Shuchi Binte Shahjalal
I asked what he wanted to be when he grew up. He said a teacher so that he could help his community get an education.
He is barely a child. And I stood there on the hillside thinking, “He is already carrying a whole community inside his plans.”
I hope someone helps him carry it. I think someone will.
A flower garden is not planted in a day. But this one has already bloomed once, where there was nothing. Somewhere beyond the river, the children are still counting.

item.title: When does a woman finally feel safe?
item.description:
Overall, with the revolutions that have taken place and the movements and policies that have been implemented, some things never seem to fully change.
The safety of a woman in Bangladesh has come down to such narrow standards that a woman would rather choose to walk alone in the pitch darkness of night on a road free of men (which is quite utopian) than walk down a street full of them in broad daylight.
Most girls are told to be home before sunset, or before it gets “too late.” The rule is ridiculous, because the risk barely changes through the day. So we are left to calculate possibilities and mentally prepare to fight off an incident, especially when commuting alone.
One question still keeps me up at night: if women are kept indoors for fear of being raped at night, why not put a curfew on men?
It is like caging the visitors at a zoo while the tiger roams free. Perhaps the guards have failed to keep the tiger caged yet have succeeded in caging the visitors.
After all, the tiger has nothing to fear. We, the humans, do.
Statistically, Bangladesh ranks very low on women’s safety, and that does not even count the thousands of incidents that go unreported.
What about the cases that never make it to the TV news?
A woman may feel unsafe in her own household at the hands of family members or relatives and still be ashamed of speaking up, because society will somehow turn the sword on her.
This is hardly rare. It is a curse to be born a woman in a society like this, in a world like this. Conditions may be improving in developed countries (though this cannot really be verified), but they represent only a small fraction of the four billion women in the world.
Even so, it is nothing to be proud of, because under regimes like the Taliban, conditions keep worsening. Women’s safety has fallen so deep it feels buried in the grave of every violated victim.
Globally, the net progress feels like zero, if not negative.
To be born a woman in a developing or underdeveloped country is to fight for rights: the right to vote and the right to education. But the intangible ones (freedom, safety, peace of mind, protection) remain neglected.
The saddest part is that the most vulnerable are often the most silenced: their hands tied in invisible chains, their mouths sealed with red tape.
These victims suffer for years, made to stay obedient in abusive households, pressured by society to preserve “dignity” and “social status” rather than speak out.
It is ultimately the fault of society and the system that continues to keep men as the dominant force.
In most households in Bangladesh, under patriarchy, the man earns money, goes outside, and makes the major financial decisions. Meanwhile, the woman is burdened with household labour, child-rearing, and unpaid labour.
It is not a choice for many women, but rather a submission to tradition.
When this continues, women-- especially those in poor and vulnerable households-- do not have the financial independence to live on their own. To them, staying in an abusive home often seems like a better option than homelessness.
In this country, marrying off a girl means her family is tension-free; it means the girl is finally handed over to someone. But why does it need to be that a woman needs someone to take care of her, such that the absence of a guard turns into a flaw?
The question still remains whether the families are actually “tension-free,” given how many marital physical abuses happen, not to mention the mental abuses as well.
It is not quite rare to see on Facebook people taking lives just because the social stigma gave no other way out of that psychological manipulation. But still, it gets normalized; be careful, though: any abuse by a man is normalized, whereas any fight/protest against that abuse is not normalized.
It is these women who have to learn it as if it is a process of natural selection, to learn to live with that misery of always being in an invisible cage, the keys to the doors never belonging to them, of course. Well, after all, in a society where teen marriages, child marriages, and polygamy are all justified, who dares to change the mindset of people?
It has been tried, but failed every time because the source cannot be uprooted; some thinking is deeply planted in patriarchy to the point that it is essential for these flaws to exist for patriarchy to continue. And for a country who has not quite seen anything else broadly other than misogyny and patriarchy, nobody is to blame.
For centuries, the vulture of victim-blaming has persisted, because it is women who have been forced to sacrifice everything just to remain accepted by society. This has conditioned many women, especially those without access to education, to believe that they are responsible for the violence done to them. That they must adjust. That they must compromise.
Life was meant to be lived by all beings. But for women, it often feels like a fragile struggle for survival, where existence itself feels like a crime.
In a country where girls are not safe at home, on the streets, in transport, or even on deathbeds, I wonder where women finally get to rest in peace --if they ever do.
Henceforth, the question always remains, “When does a woman finally feel safe?” Or perhaps safety was never meant for us--only endurance was.
Labiba Tasnim is a student in 12th grade at S.F.X. Greenherald International School in Bangladesh.

item.title: Research highlights pathways to scale up early childhood development in Bangladesh
item.description:
Early childhood development support delivered through existing public services has shown potential to improve parenting practices and home-based learning, although effective expansion requires stronger quality assurance, supervision and workforce support.
Evidence from the THRIVE Programme highlighted how existing public platforms can be used to deliver early childhood development (ECD) support while identifying key challenges to its effective implementation at scale.
The findings were presented at the national research dissemination event titled “Early Childhood Development in Bangladesh and the Way Forward” in Dhaka on Monday, attended by policymakers, researchers and development partners.
Dr Jena Derakhshani Hamadani, Emeritus Scientist at icddr,b and National Principal Investigator of the THRIVE Programme, presented the research findings and lessons.
Building on previous evidence, the Strengthening Bangladeshi Babies’ Brains (SB3) Programme expanded early childhood development activities through more than 600 Community Clinics, reaching over 15,000 children and training around 1,950 frontline health workers and more than 400 supervisors.
A recent cluster-randomized trial found significant improvements in parenting practices, home stimulation and access to play materials among intervention families. However, no statistically significant differences were found in child-development outcomes.
The findings highlight that expanding reach alone may not be sufficient to achieve the intended impact without consistent implementation, effective supervision and continued support.
Dr Tahmeed Ahmed, Executive Director of icddr,b, highlighted the close connection between nutrition and early brain development. He noted that poor nutrition during the early years can affect brain development and cognition, underscoring the need to support both children's nutrition and development during this critical period.
Dr S M Ziauddin Hyder, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Health Affairs, attended the event as the chief guest and stressed the need to take early childhood development services to national scale.
“We now have substantial evidence on the importance of early childhood development. Research shows that play-based learning, cognitive stimulation and regular interaction can significantly support children's intellectual development, with benefits that continue into later stages of learning,” he said.
Highlighting Bangladesh's learning challenges, he called for a nationwide plan to expand early childhood development activities and reach children and families across the country.
Mohammad Golam Kibria, Team Leader and Education Adviser at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), said national scale-up should focus not only on reaching more children but also on maintaining service quality.
“Scaling up must mean more than reaching larger numbers. It must also protect quality, strengthen frontline capacity, secure sustainable financing and build government ownership,” he said.
A K M Fazluzzoha, Managing Director of the Community Clinic Health Support Trust, appreciated icddr,b's work supporting children and mothers through healthcare facilities and highlighted the importance of building on this experience to expand early childhood development services nationally.
The discussions identified several priorities for the next phase, including stronger supervision and monitoring, adequate frontline capacity, continued caregiver engagement, sustainable financing and government ownership.
The THRIVE Programme is funded by the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office through its Global Research and Technology Development portfolio and the New Zealand Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and is managed by Oxford Policy Management.

item.title: DU hosts 4th Trans-Himalaya communication conference
item.description:
The 4th Trans-Himalaya Communication and Social Development Conference began at the University of Dhaka on Sunday, bringing together more than 100 academics, researchers, media professionals and young scholars from across Asia and beyond to explore regional cooperation in the era of digital intelligence.
The four-day conference, running until November 11, is jointly organised by the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, the University of Dhaka, Kangba TV and Himalaya Television.
Participants from China, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, India, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, the United States and Canada are taking part in the event themed "International Communication and Regional Development Governance in the Trans-Himalaya Region in the Era of Digital Intelligence".
Discussions are focusing on cross-border communication, regional development, climate risks, artificial intelligence, misinformation and the role of media in building public trust.
Photo: Courtesy
Speakers at the opening ceremony highlighted communication and trust as key to strengthening regional ties, stressing the need for reliable information, inclusive narratives and platforms that encourage dialogue across national and cultural boundaries.
The conference follows an interdisciplinary approach, bringing together academic research and media experience. Keynote sessions are examining issues ranging from Gandhian humanist thought and digital social transformation to regional cooperation on climate risks and combating misinformation in the age of artificial intelligence.
Six sub-forums are being held on regional coordinated development, platform algorithms and information risks, youth and public expression, cross-border communication, media industry cooperation, and ethnic exchange and integration.
A dedicated media forum is also bringing together representatives from media organisations in China, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan and other countries to discuss media credibility, public trust and professional responsibility in building a regional community.
Organisers highlighted joint programme production between Kangba TV and Himalaya Television as an example of regional media collaboration, saying such initiatives could help strengthen cross-border storytelling and promote diverse regional perspectives.
Having previously been held in China and Nepal, the conference's latest edition in Bangladesh is expected to lay the groundwork for a more regular regional dialogue mechanism, with participating countries potentially taking turns hosting future editions.
Alongside the discussions, the organisers have arranged a media industry study tour in Bangladesh, a "Himalayan Charms" photo and video exhibition, a "Humanistic China" book exhibition and a documentary showcase.

item.title: DSCC administrator urges capacity-based disaster response
item.description:
Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) Administrator Bir Muktijoddha Md Abdus Salam has called for coordinated efforts among the Fire Service, police, Red Crescent and other agencies to ensure public safety during emergencies.
He made the call while chairing the fifth meeting of the DSCC Disaster Management Committee at Nagar Bhaban on Monday afternoon, said a press release.
Abdus Salam said disaster preparedness must reflect the rescue equipment and operational capabilities of each agency, rather than remain limited to paper-based responsibility sharing.
Highlighting the unplanned development of much of Dhaka South, he stressed the need for joint efforts, regular drills and public awareness programs to reduce risks from fires, building collapses and earthquakes.
Referring to the recent fire at Moulvibazar in Old Dhaka, he said narrow roads, water shortages and roadside shops and vendors had hampered firefighters' access to the scene.
He said high-rise buildings and commercial establishments must have basic firefighting equipment and fire hydrants. He also called for underground installation of overhead cables and the preservation of ponds and water bodies, including those in Dholaikhal, to ensure adequate water for firefighting.
The meeting, attended by 57 representatives of government and private organizations, NGOs, and social organizations, also discussed agencies' responsibilities before, during, and after disasters.

item.title: US-Bangla Airlines consecutively achieves ‘Best Domestic Airline of the Year-2026’
item.description:
US-Bangla Airlines has been awarded the "Best Domestic Airline of the Year-2026" by The Bangladesh Monitor, a fortnightly travel magazine in Bangladesh, in recognition of enhancing domestic air connectivity and maintaining stability in the country's civil aviation sector.
At the award ceremony, US-Bangla also received recognition as the Best Wage Earner Friendly Airline, Best Short Haul Airline, Best Airport Service (Domestic), Popular Airline Brand in Bangladesh, Outstanding Community Service, Best Regional Airline, and Best Improved Airline.
Shafiqul Islam, head of sales at US-Bangla Airlines, received the "Best Domestic Airline of the Year-2026" award from chief guest Nasser Rahman, MP.
The awards were officially presented on November 8, 2026, at Crown Plaza Dhaka Airport.
Among other distinguished guests present at the event were Nurunnahar Chowdhury, secretary of Civil Aviation and Tourism, and Kazi Wahidul Alam, editor of The Bangladesh Monitor.
Additionally, US-Bangla Airlines received Gold awards in the categories of Best Airport Service (Domestic), Best Popular Airline Brand in Bangladesh, and Best Improved Airline, and Silver awards in the Best Short Haul, Best Wage Earner Friendly Airline, Best Outstanding Connectivity Service, and Best Regional Airline categories.
These awards from various categories were received from the guests by AKM Junaid, director of customer service; Md Kamrul Islam, general manager of Public Relations; and Iqbal Ahmed, manager of central reservations at US-Bangla Airlines.
Following the Monitor Airline of the Year 2026 awards, Mohammed Abdullah Al Mamun, managing director of US-Bangla Airlines, stated: "This recognition for US-Bangla Airlines is a reflection of the trust placed in us by our passengers. Such accolades pledge US-Bangla Airlines to do even better moving forward."
US-Bangla Airlines was previously honored with the 'Best Domestic Airline' award by The Bangladesh Monitor in 2025, 2024, 2023, 2022, and 2015.
